title: Reconstruction from the simply connected adjoint cover and the centre
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Reductivity and maximal tori have the meanings of [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. The centre $Z(G)$ is the subgroup functor of points commuting with every point after every commutative algebra extension. Quotients are represented fppf sheaf quotients as in [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. Let $G$ be reductive. Let $S$ be a perfect semisimple group, and let $q:S\to G/Z(G)$ be a universal multiplicative covering whose kernel is $Z(S)$. Perfect means that the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism factors is the whole group. Semisimple means smooth and connected with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup; solvable means that iterated commutator subgroup schemes become trivial. Universal multiplicative covering means a faithfully flat homomorphism with finite central diagonalizable kernel such that for every faithfully flat $p:E\to G/Z(G)$ with finite central diagonalizable kernel and smooth connected $E$, there is a unique $u:S\to E$ satisfying $p\circ u=q$. A diagonalizable group is $D_F(M)=\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ for a finitely generated abelian group $M$, with group algebra basis $e_m$, multiplication $e_me_n=e_{m+n}$ and comultiplication $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$ [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality]. Then $D=Z(G)$ is diagonalizable and there exists $v:S\to G$ lifting $q$. Its restriction $\varphi:Z(S)\to D$ has torus cokernel, and the homomorphism $S\times D\to G$, $(s,d)\mapsto v(s)d$, identifies $G$ with the fppf quotient $$G\simeq(S\times D)/\{(z,\varphi(z)^{-1}):z\in Z(S)\}.$$ Here torus means isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some $r\geq0$, with $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Moreover $G^{\mathrm{der}}=\operatorname{im}(v)\simeq S/\ker\varphi$ as subgroup schemes of $G$, where $G^{\mathrm{der}}$ denotes the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism factors. The homomorphism $\varphi$ is not required to be injective or trivial. The statement includes the trivial group and all characteristics.

source.place: Definition 19.26, Proposition 19.27, Example 19.25 and Remark 19.30, printed pp.404--405. Use the simply connected covering in Remark 19.30, allowing a noninjective homomorphism on centres; Proposition 19.27 identifies the derived subgroup and torus quotient.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change], $D=Z(G)$ is a closed normal commutative subgroup. Choose a Borel subgroup using the existence assertion of [lem-sfb-borel-conjugation-cover], then a split maximal torus $T$ using [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy]. For every algebra $A$ and every $z\in D(A)$, the definition of the centre makes $z$ commute with all $T(A')$ after every $A$-algebra extension. Hence $D\subseteq C_G(T)=T$ by [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer]. This is a closed subgroup inclusion: the surjection $F[G]\to F[D]$ factors through $F[T]$. Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] to obtain $D\simeq D_F(M)$. No root datum or rank-one classification is used.

source.place: Corollary 17.62(a), Proposition 17.61(a), p.372; Theorem 17.10, pp.354--355; Theorem 12.9(c), pp.233--234.

proof.text: Put $H=G^{\mathrm{der}}$. By [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup] it is smooth, connected and normal. Form the closed image $I$ of $D\times H\to G$ using [lem-sfb-affine-homomorphism-flat-image]. Centrality of $D$ and normality of $H$ show that $I$ is normal (conjugate local expressions $dh$). By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] the quotient $G/I$ exists; it is commutative since it kills $H$. It also kills $D$, so its quotient map factors through $Q=G/D$. The resulting map $S\xrightarrow{q}Q\to G/I$ is trivial: its kernel contains all commutators of the perfect group $S$. As $q$ is an fppf epimorphism, $Q\to G/I$ is trivial, and therefore $G/I=1$. Thus $G=DH$ and multiplication $D\times H\to G$ is faithfully flat. These equalities mean equality of fppf sheaves and closed subgroup schemes.

source.place: Example 19.25, p.404: the common commutative and perfect quotient argument, using the given perfect covering S instead of Corollary 21.50.

proof.text: Set $K=D\cap H$. Apply [lem-sfb-central-diagonalizable-derived-intersection-finite] to the smooth connected $G$ and central diagonalizable $D$ of step 1: $K$ is finite. It is diagonalizable by [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable], since it is a closed subgroup of the split torus $T$ from step 1. The restriction $p:H\to Q$ has kernel $K$ and is an fppf epimorphism: locally lift a point of $Q$ to $g\in G$, then write $g=dh$ by step 2. The quotient statements of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] identify $H/K\simeq Q$ and make $p$ faithfully flat. Its kernel is central, finite and diagonalizable and its source $H$ is smooth and connected. The stipulated universal property of $q$ therefore gives $u:S\to H$ with $pu=q$. Define $v$ as $S\xrightarrow{u}H\hookrightarrow G$.

source.place: Remark 19.30, p.405, lifting through the multiplicative isogeny of Example 19.25; Proposition 12.46(a), pp.245--246.

proof.text: For $z\in Z(S)$, $q(z)=1$, so $v(z)\in\ker(G\to Q)=D$. Define $\varphi=v|_{Z(S)}$. The homomorphism $m:S\times D\to G$, $m(s,d)=v(s)d$, is fppf locally surjective: for any $g$, lift its image in $Q$ locally to $s\in S$, and put $d=v(s)^{-1}g\in D$. Its kernel on every algebra is exactly $\{(z,\varphi(z)^{-1}):z\in Z(S)\}$, because $m(s,d)=1$ implies $q(s)=1$, and the assumed scheme-theoretic kernel of $q$ is $Z(S)$. The inverse-diagonal graph is closed and central. The fppf quotient universal property of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] now identifies $G$ with the stated quotient of $S\times D$. This computation uses all algebra-valued points, not just field-valued points.

source.place: Definition 19.26 and Remark 19.30, pp.404--405; explicit kernel calculation in their defining diagram.

proof.text: Let $J=\operatorname{im}(v)\subseteq H$ be the closed faithfully flat image furnished by [lem-sfb-affine-homomorphism-flat-image]. From step 4, every point of $G$ is fppf locally $v(s)d$. Hence each commutator of points of $G$ is locally $v([s_1,s_2])$, so lies in $J$; membership in a closed subgroup descends along an fppf cover. Consequently the commutator morphism factors through $J$ and the defining minimality of $H$ gives $H\subseteq J$. Since $J\subseteq H$, $J=H$. Thus $u:S\to H$ is faithfully flat. Its kernel is $\ker\varphi$: an element killed by $v$ is killed by $q$ and hence lies in $Z(S)$, where $v=\varphi$. Applying [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to $S/\ker\varphi$ gives $H\simeq S/\ker\varphi$ with the required inclusion into $G$.

source.place: Proposition 19.27, pp.404--405, derived-subgroup identification; commutator computation for the quotient from step 4.

proof.text: Since $u:S\to H$ is fppf locally surjective, every $k\in K$ lifts fppf locally to $s\in S$ with $v(s)=k$. Then $q(s)=1$, so $s\in Z(S)$. Conversely $v(Z(S))\subseteq K$. Therefore $\operatorname{im}\varphi=K$ as fppf sheaves. Step 2 also gives $D/K\simeq G/H$: $D\to G/H$ is locally surjective with kernel $K$, so [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] identifies these quotients. That same node says $G/H$ is smooth and connected. The quotient $D/K$ is diagonalizable by [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-quotient-character-kernel], and a smooth connected group of multiplicative type is a torus by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus]. Over the algebraically closed $F$ this is $\mathbf G_m^r$. Thus $\operatorname{coker}\varphi=D/K$ is a torus, as claimed. Nothing asserts that $\varphi$ is injective, or that its finite image is reduced.

(2) G=Z(G)G^der follows from the perfect S and the faithfully flat q, since G/I is commutative and is killed by S. (3) K=D∩H is finite by new node 1 and diagonalizable inside T; H/K≅G/Z(G); the item's universal property applies to the smooth connected H and gives u. (4) The kernel of (s,d)↦v(s)d is the inverse-diagonal graph because ker q=Z(S); the elementary mark is accepted. (5) Commutators of G are locally v([s1,s2]), so J=H and ker u=ker φ. (6) im φ=K and D/K≅G/H is smooth and connected; D/K is diagonalizable by new node 2 and hence a torus by the largest-subtorus node.
